utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Wednesday, and I greet everyone here in the courtroom, the accused, the Defence counsel, our witness, Mr. Kruger, Mr. Stringer, and everyone helping them, as well as all those assisting us. We are starting six minutes late. We're not to blame, because I was at the door of this courtroom at 2.00 p.m. sharp, but the Gotovina Trial Chamber once again, despite all the warnings we've given them, went beyond the time allotted, as usual. So all my apologies for this, but we're not to blame for this situation, and I will seize the President of the Tribunal of this problem. Now, I believe that the Registrar has an IC number to give us. He has the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Petkovic Defence has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to its lists of documents tendered through Witness Ivan Beneta. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01115. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Kruger, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to Your Honours, and good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Pavlovic, good afternoon to you. Let's start by very quickly just revisiting part of your evidence from yesterday and the day before, and this relates to the 30 June 1993 order by General Petkovic for the isolation of all Muslim men in your units, and then military-aged men as well. Now, you were asked about the fact that Brigadier Lasic had forwarded this order to various units under his command, but not to the 1st Knez Domagoj Brigade. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, given the fact that you also testified that elements from this order did come down to you for implementation, wouldn't you say that it's entirely plausible that Brigadier Lasic had also provided this order to Nedjeljko Obradovic separately or by another means?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier Lasic could have sent the order to Colonel Obradovic separately or by some other means, perhaps even orally, but from the document, as far as I remember, he didn't send him that kind of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's turn very briefly, then, also to the briefing that you had in Domanovici on the evening of the 30th of June. And for this, I would like you to turn to Exhibit P03038. It's in your binder, and it's about the 12th or 13th document in the binder. 3038. Sir, the --

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you help me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I could explain. The tabs that you see are in chronological order, even though they're not in sequence.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this document is dated the 30th of June, 1993, and it's a proclamation issued by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, as president of the HZ-HB HVO, we'll see at the end, and by Mr. Bruno Stojic, head of HZ-HB Defence Department, and this was issued on the day of the attack on the North Barracks. And if we just look at the very first paragraph of the document, it says: "In relation to the new attack carried out by the Muslim forces of the HVO --" or "on the HVO positions and the Croatian people that live in this area, with which continues the war of conquest that started in the territory of Central Bosnia, the Chairman of the Croatian Defence Council, Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and head of the Defence Department of the Croatian Defence Council, Mr. Bruno Stojic, sent the following message to the Croatian people that live in Herceg-Bosnia." And if we look at the addressees or whom it's submitted to, it says: All heads of the HVO municipalities; all officers for defence of municipalities; military police command and civil police administration, and media. Sir, on the evening -- well, first of all, let me ask you this: Are you aware of this proclamation? Do you recall it from that period of time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite frank, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's look at the text of this, and in your version, the original B/C/S version, I think it's the last paragraph on the first page. And in the English version, it's the paragraph starting with: "Brothers Croats ..." It says: "Brothers Croats, in --" sorry. Just before that, the previous paragraph describes what had happened at the Tihomir Misic Barracks and gives an interpretation of the events, and then it says: "Brothers Croats, in this crucial moment for our people, the only thing that can make us survive is the utmost patriotism and higher goals of the Croatian survival, wherever our homes were built for centuries." "We should unite all our forces from every Croatian village and town from the whole Herceg-Bosnia in order to stop the Muslim aggression. Croats from Siroki Brijeg, Posusje, Citluk, Grude, Livno, Tomislavgrad, Capljina, Stolac, and other HZ-HB municipalities. Mostar was and remained the Croatian town." Sir, wasn't this document also discussed or put -- or made known at the briefing at Domanovici on the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that last question of yours? I was reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this document, with its appeal, wasn't this discussed or put to everybody at the briefing of the 30th of June in Domanovici that you attended?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. And from the addressees, that is, to whom this document was sent, it could only have been made public through the information media, because I see that the media was sent a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, in the piece that we've just read, it also says: "We should unite all our forces from every Croatian village and town ..." From the next day onwards -- well, we've seen documents over the past two days where military commanders are also giving orders to the military police and the civilian police. From what you read here, if this document was, indeed, issued, or this proclamation, do you think it's entirely possible -- would you agree that it's entirely possible that this is an indication where the authorisation comes from the military to also employ military police and civilian police members or units?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would object on the grounds of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm putting the question, and I think that the witness is entirely capable of answering the question, given his own position and relatively senior position at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gentleman has indicated he's never seen the document. Now he's being asked to speculate as to whether something in this document could have done something else. Frankly, the answer is irrelevant, because he has no basis for the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, this witness is a senior officer, and he is well able to say, I don't know this document, I cannot answer your question. And if he can answer, well, he will. Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, because only part of the document was read out to the witness. The witness, himself, said he's never seen the whole document. On page 2 of this document, there's a portion which could relate to the question asked by the Prosecutor. So the question by the Prosecutor has been construed with the excerpts read out, and I think that it is very important, when he mentions Mostar as the main city, the last -- or capital city, that it was the international factors who recognised this, and that is in the last sentence. So the second part of the document can be linked with the military and civilian police, so only a partial reading of this document to the witness, who says he's never seen the document, can lead the witness to give the wrong answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kruger. I must, to some degree, agree with Mr. Karnavas. I find your question very complex with all, "is there a possibility," "that there is a possibility that maybe." And I cannot make much sense of it, I must confess, so perhaps you better completely reformulate or go to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I won't belabour this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I would actually prefer to return to the whole issue of the Bregava Brigade, sir. Now, yesterday we concluded the examination, and we were exploring the notion of whether the Bregava Brigade and its members had a legitimate expectation or right to operate on the territory of Stolac municipality. And we touched upon that Bregava Brigade wanting a larger role, and my contention to you or what I put to you as well was that it was actually being side-lined by the HVO, being prevented from assuming that role. I'd like to continue looking at this aspect. For this, I don't think we need to turn to this document, but you recall that over the past two days there has been reference to an order by Miljenko Lasic on the 6th of December, 1992, and it was the order assigning certain positions to the Bregava Brigade and then also allowing the Bregava Brigade to establish a headquarters in Prenj. Do you remember that, that we have looked at that document, that we spoke about it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly which document that was in, but the Bregava Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Prenj is at a distance from the front-line of over 20 kilometres, and the -- if you take the road, it's longer, so it's 20 kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreter has asked that you repeat the first part of your question -- of your answer. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that I can't remember what document you're referring to, but I do know that the brigade, the Bregava Brigade, never got the village of Prenj as a command post, nor did it -- nor was the command post ever installed in the village of Prenj. And the Bregava Brigade was given a part of the defence line around Prenj, that is to say, 15 kilometres away as the crow flies, and if you take the road, then it's over 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kruger. Mr. Pavlovic, could you explain where the front-line was, maybe at least by naming villages? Like Djelojevici [phoen], would that be a place where the front-line was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm -- I can tell you all the places through which the front-line passed in that area, if we start out from Golo Brdo -- Golo Brda, which is before Bijelo Jevici [phoen], those are positions in front of the village of Bjelovici at a distance of 3 to 5 kilometres. And then it passed along Drenovac, in front of Drenovac. And then the line went further along across a place called Poprat. It's an area comprising several villages. And then it passed along the cemetery, had a central position in front of Poprat at the cemetery. And then it passed by the village of Ravnice, and the village of Basilije, and then the village of Komonje [phoen] Brdo, and between the villages of Lozanici [phoen] and Barane [phoen], through the village of Hodovo or, rather, the outer-reaches of Hodovo, in front of the village of Rotimlje, and then it passed in front of the village of Vranici in the Kameni area, and then Podvelezje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, that's quite helpful. Please, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's quickly, then, indeed turn to the document of the 12th of December, and it is the fourth document in your binder, the fourth one from the beginning, and it is document P00868. Sir, you need to look at the pages on the right -- left side of your binder. Sir, you're looking at the wrong place.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't found it. Would you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: P00868. If you close your binder -- thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I apologise. I've found it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this is the order 6th December 1992 by Miljenko Lasic, and we see that it -- the addressees are: The Bregava Brigade, Stolac, Southern Barracks, and then copied to the 1st Brigade and the 3rd Brigade. And we see the order is simply for organisation of combat activities at the battle-field in the municipalities of Mostar and Stolac. "I hereby issue the following order: "The Bregava Brigade is to take over the responsibility for the following defence line," and then gives a location. And then if we look at the second-to-last paragraph of the order, it says: "The unit is to be accommodated in the Prenj locality (school or any other suitable structure.)" And it's correct this is what we were talking about earlier and what you had already said that this was, indeed, accurate, or this order was issued by Mr. Lasic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from this we can see that the order was issued by Mr. Lasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we turn to the very next document, which is P01402. And we see that this is a document from about a month later, and it's the 23rd of -- or at least it says at the end the document is -- the order is to be carried out on the 23rd of January, 1993. It's an order by Miljenko Lasic, and what I'd like to point you to is point number 3, which says: "The location for headquarters and the reserve unit," and this would be of the Bregava Brigade, "is to be organised exclusively in one of the barracks or in the military building in the area of the Operational Zone South-East Herzegovina and according to the arrangement agreed with the commander of the Operational Zone South-East Herzegovina." My question, sir, is: This is five, six weeks after the order of the 6th of December, and is it correct that at this stage the Bregava Brigade had still not established a headquarters in Prenj?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Bregava Brigade never set up headquarters in Prenj. I can confirm that. And I can also confirm that the positions stated here are ones that I know very well, because they're located in the place that I was born and where I live today. And I can also confirm one other thing, and that is my professional military opinion, because I know the situation from that time, and it is something that became clear to everybody later on, but at the time when this first order was issued, the Bregava Brigade was not capable of holding these positions because it was only a brigade in name, whereas the actual brigade didn't resemble any other proper brigades either by the number of soldiers or by virtue of some other attributes that a brigade must have. And so because it was incapable of taking these positions, as far as I know, in the area of Kotarznica [phoen], which is a very sensitive area, a very difficult area to hold, then they gave them some other positions, that is to say, to the left of that area, small positions. When I say "small," I mean an area of 500 to 600 metres, at the most. And the Bregava Brigade held that for a time, and in the action by the Serb forces that we mentioned earlier on, it lost those positions. And this is yet further confirmation of my observations that the Bregava Brigade at that time was truly not properly capacitated to be able to hold those positions. And if I might be allowed to add -- may I continue, please? Then I can tell you a few facts which would make the situation clearer to you, the situation in that particular unit. So may I do that? Can I go on to explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Can I first ask you this, sir: Is it correct that the 1st Knez Domagoj Brigade of the HVO, and the commander, Mr. Nedjeljko Obradovic, that they were actually also opposed to the Bregava Brigade situating its headquarters on the territory of Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My understanding of the situation dating back to those times is as follows: The 1st Brigade, to which I belonged, in part, did not want nor could it take in any other unit in the central area of responsibility and be held responsible for the defence lines. I'd never allow myself to be in that position, especially if I was certain that that particular unit could not perform its assignment properly. And that unit, in actual fact, at that time was incapable of carrying out its combat assignment, and I can state the reasons for that to make the situation clearer to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Before you say that, what period are you referring to, specifically, that they were not capable of performing these assignments?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they weren't able to carry out the assignments from their very establishment, from -- until they were established first and until they were disbanded, because they didn't engage in those assignments at all. It was just a pretext for something else that they were doing. Now, if you would like me to tell you, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Actually, I do want to explore this, but perhaps I'm going to ask you questions and we'll see if we get the information you want to provide. You mentioned -- a part of your testimony yesterday and the day before yesterday was that the Bregava Brigade -- you had intelligence reports indicating plans of the Bregava Brigade to break off co-operation with the HVO and to start combat actions with the HVO. You remember your evidence to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what exactly this refers to. Could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, I'll explain. And your testimony was specifically that upon the arrest of members of the Bregava Brigade and the command, documents were found with the command which completely confirmed the intelligence reports. Moreover, those documents proved that the BiH Army planned to carry out its offensive actions against the HVO in co-operation with HV soldiers of Muslim ethnicity. And then you were shown a number of documents showing an order by Bajro Pizovic on the 5th of April, for instance, ordering heightened combat readiness, and then a series of documents after that. Do you recall that testimony of yours?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I would like to ask my learned friend to provide a reference to the page where this very answer of the witness was recorded, because I must admit that my recollection of his answer is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I was reading from the summary provided, so it is, indeed, a bit of a paraphrasing, perhaps. But I don't think it's contentious that that was the nature of the evidence that he gave or the tenure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the summary that we submitted to our colleagues in the Prosecution and then the other Defence counsels are my rendering of the events and not the very words uttered in this courtroom, so we have to be vigilant because the witness did not state that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, if you were unclear, do rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, a number of documents were shown to you on Monday evening pertaining to April, and these documents were, for instance: 4D01809. We needn't look at the document, but it's a 5 April order by Bajro Pizovic for the Bregava Brigade to increase its level of combat readiness. And then there were other orders: 5D03046, an order by Pizovic on 15 April; there was an order on 16th April, 4D0033. But the point that was being made by these documents was that the Bregava Brigade was planning an offensive against the HVO in Stolac, and where these documents came from was that these documents were obtained from the records of the Bregava Brigade Command, if I'm not mistaken. Do you recall that or is this a correct rendering of that evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot precisely say which documents these are, but I agree that on Monday we saw a series of documents from which it could be seen that the Bregava Brigade was planning to launch offensive actions against the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And these documents, would you agree that they generally dated from the period of -- or from April 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to then turn to the next document, and this is four documents further on in your bind. It's Exhibit P01804, P01804. This is a document which is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 04, one down here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That's correct, if you turn to the B/C/S version, the translated version. This, sir, is a media report, and it's dated the 4th of April, 1993. The headline is: "Bosnian Croats Demand Muslim Troop Pull-Outs." You're looking at the English. If you could turn to the B/C/S version, sir. Yes. At the top, it's "4 April 1993, Sunday." Headline: "Bosnian Croats Demand Troop Pull-Outs." And then it says: "Body." It says, the first paragraph: "Bosnian Croats on Sunday demanded the withdrawal of Muslim troops from the provinces designated for Croat self-rule under a UN peace plan, reviving tensions between nominal civil war allies who battled early this year." Now, sir, first of all before continuing, if we look at that paragraph, you wouldn't disagree that this UN peace plan is a reference to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we don't need to read this whole report, but if you go one, two, three, four -- the fifth paragraph of this document, it says: "The HVO set an April 15 dead-line for Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic to sign a joint communique ratifying the withdrawals, creating a common high command, and certifying there were no Muslim-Croat territorial disputes." And then if we go down two paragraphs further, it says: "'If Izetbegovic fails to sign this agreement by 15 April, the HVO will unilaterally enforce its jurisdiction in Cantons 3, 8, and 10,' the statement from HVO headquarters in south-west Croat stronghold of Mostar warned." And then the next paragraph it says that the Croatian Radio has reported that Mate Boban had already signed the proposed communique. Sir, were you aware of an ultimate issued by Mr. Boban on the 4th of April, 1993, to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, Stolac, you don't dispute that that was actually intended to be part of Province 8 in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And so if this ultimatum indeed was issued, would you agree that its implication for Muslim units, such as the Bregava Brigade, on the territory of Stolac would be that they would, by 15 April, either have to disarm or perhaps even leave the territory of Stolac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about such an ultimatum. This is the assessment of a journalist, and as far as I can tell, he is referring to statements uttered at Croatian Radio Mostar or any other radio station, so I cannot confirm that there, indeed, was an ultimatum, and I haven't heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, indeed there is other evidence before the Chamber also of this ultimatum, but my question is: If this ultimatum existed, that would have the effect that by the 15th of April, the Bregava Brigade may have to either totally disarm or leave the territory of Stolac municipality; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me this objection as regards the factual basis for this question. If the witness doesn't know about the so-called ultimatum, and if he is not familiar with all its elements, then he cannot reply to this question, because the question does not offer all the options that, according to the Prosecutor, were part of that ultimatum. So I believe it would be useful for all of us if that could be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Objection overruled. This is a hypothesis which is absolutely graspable, and it does not ask the witness to make any factual actual assertion. Please continue, Mr. Kruger. The Chamber has ruled, Ms. Alaburic. This is a ruling of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I absolutely accept. I have no intention of reiterating my objection. But if you let me explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't want any explanation. The Prosecutor asked a question of the witness. The witness answered, and he said he wasn't aware of the ultimatum. And so he said -- what else do you want? Now, you're shooting yourself in the foot if you intervene. He said he didn't know, so the Prosecutor is going to try and make him understand that he's lying, that he knew, or that he doesn't want to say anything, because if you intervene, you weaken the witness's answers. That's what I don't understand. You're calling the witness for your own case. As long as the witness doesn't testify against you, let him do his job. He said he didn't know about any ultimatum. Why did you take the floor, all the more so since you're going to have re-examination and you can always return -- revisit the issue if you're not happy with the witness's answers? By taking the floor, you're just sort of working against yourself. I don't understand. And the Prosecutor is allowed to present his case. He believes that there was an ultimatum. The witness answers that there wasn't any. So let's go along and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do consider it necessary to say now that I am not objecting to the answers provided by the witness, but I consider it my duty to object to the question. And if the question is referring to a factual basis and it is incomplete, I think it is my duty to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer the question, which basically is that: If this ultimatum was in existence, wouldn't its effect be that the members of the Bregava Brigade would most likely have to disarm and then, even by 15 April, have to leave the territory of Stolac? Wouldn't that be the implication?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat once more that I truly don't know of such an ultimatum. If it had been issued in any form, I don't believe that the units in the same combat disposition -- or that had been in the same combat disposition for quite a time, would have disarmed, because weakening the defence line is something that nobody could have ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: We'll look at that in just a moment. But, sir, the members of this Bregava Brigade, you'd already said most of them were from Stolac municipality. Would you agree, sir, if an ultimatum such as this had been issued, that those men would rightly have felt very worried about their immediate future and what would happen to them on 15 April, when the ultimatum expired? Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that those people had no reason to worry at all, because if they had kept their area of responsibility and if their command hadn't continuously provoked, they would never have been moved from there. Probably as the brigade would have grown in size and strength, it would have been assigned a greater zone of responsibility. Nobody would have considered it in their interest to remove a unit which lived up to its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that an order such as that issued by Bajro Pizovic on April 5 for the heightened combat readiness of members of the Bregava Brigade was a direct response to this ultimatum which had been issued by Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the response to the constant warnings of the brigade commander that they must leave the zone of responsibility of the 1st Herzegovina Brigade, the command post of which was at the Gubavica village, and that they must take the zone assigned to them and return to their command post, which is the Juzni Logor Barracks. And all orders sent out by the Bregava Brigade commander were about such warnings, and I know of no other warnings but that they were being warned that they must leave the zone of responsibility of the 1st Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's have a very brief look at what, indeed, happened the day after the expiry of the ultimatum, and this would have been on the 16th of April, 1993. And you were shown, in this regard -- or you were shown on Monday evening two documents, and they are -- and I don't think we need to turn to them. You'll recall them because you confirmed them. Two orders by Nedjeljko Obradovic, P01900 and then P01913. What these orders are about, both on 16 April, they're orders to disarm and detain ABiH members, and ABiH members are not to be allowed into the Knez Domagoj area of responsibility. Do you recall those two orders?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this refers to that request and the order that are almost identical. We spoke about that yesterday. The "01" sequence was missing in one of them. And I'm sure that at that moment, nobody went to disarm the Bregava Brigade, but rather that this applied to members not only of the Bregava Brigade, but members of all other units which, without any permission and no approval, entered the zone of the 1st Herzegovina Brigade. And I can confirm some other allegations, too. At that time, we really made efforts for the relations between the HVO and the ABiH to be good, and if you remember my order which I interpreted yesterday, it grew out of the agreement between me and the commander of the Bregava Brigade, Mr. Bajro Pizovic, during his stay at Stolac. To make it clearer to you, above the command, where the forward command post of Stolac was, I believe on the second or third storey of that building - I'm not sure which - in one of the apartments there was the headquarters of the SDA party, and as Mr. Pizovic was one of the vice-presidents of the party, he called at that place often and he had no difficulties in going through HVO positions or passing through. But his soldiers would leave their positions often without permission, and he would then send military police from his ranks. And under the pretext of collecting his soldiers, he would he would also pick up a dozen or so young Muslims from the town of Stolac or from the municipality and mobilise them by force, and their families complained. Some even came to our command to complain, and I insisted that Mr. Pizovic stop doing that. I tried to agree with him, in a gentleman-like fashion, and we said that if a soldier of the ABiH leaves his positions, without the permission of the commander of the Bregava Brigade, and goes into his place of residence, he should issue a request to our command and we will send out military police that will search out that soldier and take him to the Aladinici check-point, where the ABiH will take him over. If anything like that should happen with a soldier of the HVO, the same will apply vice versa. And this agreement was honoured for a while, but then came a day when that came to an end, and probably the brigade commander saw himself forced to issue such an order. So that's what things were really like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we'll come back to that in one moment. Just to complete, then, on this topic: This is your view now, that actually the HVO was acting reasonably; it was the Bregava Brigade which was acting unreasonably and which was provoking. I put to you, sir, that actually the orders of 16 April 1993 by Colonel Obradovic were actually in execution of the ultimatum by Mate Boban. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that in any case, but, of course, I cannot prevent you from having your own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. And just one further item. Two other orders were also shown to you, and these were documents 4D00033 of 16 April and 4D00034 of 18 April 1993, and these were calls to Muslims in the HVO to side with the ABiH. Do you recall seeing those two documents?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If possible, I would ask you to show them to me, because there have been many documents and it's difficult to remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may ask the assistance of the usher to perhaps just show the original to the witness, if we could, perhaps. I have them here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I know what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the only point I want to put to you on these is that: If the ultimatum by Mr. Boban indeed existed, then the call by Mr. Pizovic and the Bregava Brigade to Muslims in the HVO to join their side, it actually then is much less sinister than it first looked; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll repeat once more that at the time I wasn't aware of any ultimatum and that any documents issued by Mr. Pizovic or his assistant - in this case it was probably Mr. Huso Maric - or, rather, declarations or proclamations issued to HVO soldiers had different goals and were not the reaction to any ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's move back to your earlier point. You said that you approached Mr. Pizovic as a gentleman. Let's have a look at an occasion where Mr. Pizovic may have been trying to approach Nedjeljko Obradovic as a gentleman. Let's look at Exhibit P01997, and it should be just the next document on from the one we've just been looking at. P019997 [sic]. Now, sir, this document, if we look at the back, it's by Commander Bajro Pizovic, and it's addressed to the Command of the 1st Herzegovina Brigade on 20 -- and it's unclear which date it is, but I think we can assume that this is the 20th of April that this was written. And I'd like to point you to the first paragraph. It says, the last sentence of the first paragraph: "Also, I felt the need to address you as my neighbour and the man who commands the HVO forces in this area, in our fight against the common enemy." "We are aware of the task which was given to the HVO forces and to units of the HV Army in this area against the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and against the Muslim people which is, unfortunately, against our wishes, and we hope also against your wishes, in conflict. "Acting in accordance with your activities, and especially after your provocations towards us, using military force, even tanks, in order to provoke us to enter into a conflict, I, together with my soldiers and with people, do not want a conflict." Now, sir, from this would you agree that Mr. Pizovic is actually saying that it is the HVO which is provoking a conflict, not the Bregava Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a few moments to just finish reading it. Mr. Pizovic here is saying -- or, rather, is stating some facts as if he were the one who was attacked. However, he also says that the HVO attacked him, units of the Croatian Defence Council. I might use a rather harsh term now, but this is quite stupid, as far as I'm concerned, because at that time there were no units of the Croatian Army in the area, which leads me to think that the other facts stated here have -- are incorrect and have been fabricated, because I don't remember that there were any similar situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I put it to you, and then we'll step off the topic, that it was the HVO which was provoking the Bregava Brigade because the Bregava Brigade created -- or was an obstacle to incorporating Stolac into the HZ-HB. They wanted to get rid of the HZ-HB. They didn't want it on the territory of Stolac. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that the Bregava Brigade could have put up any obstacles to anyone, because as I said a moment ago -- well, I described the unit to you. It was a unit which was incapable of standing up to anybody, and even the positions that we assigned to it, which it was supposed to hold and a company could hold it, they weren't able to do that, let alone to appear as some kind of authority able to defend Stolac. So I can't agree with that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I, Mr. Kruger. Mr. Pavlovic, I seem to detect a certain contradiction in what you have told us this afternoon, because in the first line of questions the Prosecutor has put it to you that the HVO wanted to get rid of the Bregava Brigade, which ought to have left the area, and you say, Oh, no, that could never have been the case because we need them for the defence. It's impossible to take them away, because that would weaken the defence. And now you say, and you have hinted at that before, They were worthless, they were completely useless. So I wonder whether you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not say -- or perhaps you didn't understand me properly. I did not say that the relations between the units of the Croatian Defence Council and the BH Army, up until the time -- or, rather, until the spring of 1993, were not good. I didn't say that. They were at a high level, at an enviable level, and we can see that from any of the documents. Relations were good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I wonder whether you've understood my question, because I didn't refer to anything like that. You have first said it would have been impossible to remove the Bregava Brigade, not ABiH in general, because it was needed to hold the lines. No reasonable commander would have withdrawn troops. Now you also say, and you have said so before, The Bregava Brigade was of no use. So it could not at the same time be necessary for the defence and of no use, no power to stand up against anybody. This is the contradiction I seem to detect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President -- I mean, Your Honour, if you can clarify the latter part. When you say "of no use," I understand what you're getting at, but I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I can, I can, although it's actually the question of whether the witness understands, not whether you understand, and I'm amazed that you don't know. But the witness has just said that the Bregava Brigade was so weak it could not stand up against anything, it could not be an obstacle. So if it can't even be an obstacle, what use can it be in defence against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I've understood your question better now. What I mean to say is this: I said that nobody wanted to remove the Bregava Brigade, but they wanted to have the Bregava Brigade act within its assigned area of responsibility. Now, when I gave my last answer, my last interpretation, I said, and it was the truth, that the Bregava Brigade lost that area of responsibility that was assigned to it and dealt with other things, altogether other things, and not what had been assigned to it, its prime tasks. And at the beginning, it's true, we wanted this brigade to be part of the defence system, to grow, and we had very proper relations with it. However, on a daily basis, as time went by, it began dealing in other affairs and not the assignments and tasks given it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It might be helpful if you could tell us a date, maybe approximate, when the Bregava Brigade lost its area of responsibility. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That happened in February. And I think in the documents we looked at, we'll be able to find the right date, but I think it was in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did they do afterwards? What was their task afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their tasks were to see to an area of responsibility that had been restricted. They were kept at the same positions, but given a smaller area of responsibility, because they lost control of Feature 690, for example, which was of enormous strategic importance for the entire area. And in Operation Bura, because of taking control of that feature, we lost dozens of soldiers and some of our legendary commanders as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me for the interruption, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in April, could you tell us whether you were commanding the 1st Brigade of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have a document on the screen. Could you tell us who it was sent to, according to you? You didn't know of this document, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'd never seen it before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wanted to put this on the transcript. This document was seemingly handed to the OTP on August 16, 2000, by Mr. Bajro Pizovic, himself, and the investigator of the OTP was probably a French speaker because this letter was translated into French, because I have a French version. But, Witness, you do not know this document. I note that the Prosecutor believes that it is dated April 20th, but in the B/C/S document we see that the date is "20.0" blank, period, so we don't know whether it's a "4" for "April." But, you might confirm, Mr. Prosecutor, you might confirm that there is no mention of ultimatum here, and there is no mention that weapons must be surrendered or that there is a need to be subordinated or re-subordinated to the HVO. Witness, can you tell us whether there is mention of all this? Is there mention of an ultimatum, a re-subordination, in this document, in the original version in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't had time to read it all, except for the paragraph that I was asked about by the Prosecutor. So might I take a moment to read through it, and then I'll be able to answer your question. But as things now stand, I can't do that. I don't see any mention of an ultimatum here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Assuming that this document was actually written in 1993, assuming, because we -- this document was handed over in 2000, so everything's possible, let's assume this is a genuine document, it would seem that at that moment there are soldiers of the Bregava Brigade or ABiH soldiers who were arrested and detained. What's your take on this? Is it true, is it false? At the almost last paragraph, there is a request for a liberation -- a release of these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's highly possible that at that time there were commanders or, rather, members of the Bregava Brigade who had been arrested and detained precisely for the reasons that we mentioned earlier on, because they often came to the positions and left them without anybody's authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. You knew Pizovic, didn't you? I think yesterday you told us that you knew this person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When reading this letter by Pizovic, I note that the tone is very moderate, it's full of respect towards the HVO, and the impression you get from this letter is that Mr. Pizovic does not like conflict and is trying to find a solution. Is it true, is it false? Does this correspond to Mr. Pizovic's personality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a letter is one thing, and the situation on the ground is something quite different again. Knowing him personally, as I do, and knowing the situation on the ground as well, I am really rather astonished that he wrote such a fine letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is what I wanted to know, and this letter is very courteous. Does this correspond to Mr. Pizovic's personality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't want to give you my personal, subjective opinion alone. We've seen many documents here that are quite different in tone from this letter, so that's how I see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if he was British, you could say he's a gentleman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's precisely written in a gentlemanly fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to very briefly touch upon the next document, not spend much time on it, and that is document P02790, and it's about four or five documents on -- further on in your binder. P02790. And, sir, this is a document -- do you have it? This is a document --

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You mean the report? It's a report; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: That's correct. It's a report of 15 June 1993, and it's signed by Mr. Zarko Pavlovic, chief of the Security Service of the Knez Domagoj 1st Brigade. My first question is: This Pavlovic being referred to is a different person; it's not mistakenly you referred to in the document?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the same surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, what this document is about -- I'm not going to go through the whole document, but what it is about, we'll look at the first paragraph: "Having gathered information on the movement or intentions of the BH Army, that is, the Bregava Brigade, about their location to Bivolje Brdo or the Stolac hospital (patients were there only until the Bregava Brigade arrived, and then the hospital should cease to exist), we thought it was the last moment to use force to make them leave to Gubavica." And then the next paragraph relates to the arrest of members of the Bregava Brigade on 19 April 1993. It says that the commanders fled Gubavica, only to be caught two days later at Osanici, and that's correct, that's what happened? You don't dispute that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes, several days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And the document continues in saying that: "On the 13th of June, the mopping up of the remaining army area at Rotimlje started," and describes that. And then, sir, what I'd like to go to is the very last paragraph -- or, well, near the bottom. It says: "By searching the terrain in depth of the brigade's zone of responsibility, we will have a real picture of the strength of the line of the Chetniks and facing the BH Army." And then this part: "Our aim is to create a situation in which the Muslims will not trust one another, which will make them easy to control."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Correction, or question. In the transcript, you read, and I've heard you say so "we'll have a real picture," page 31, line 10, "a real picture of the strength of the line of the Chetniks," and I read in the document "a strength of the line facing the Chetniks," which would be the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. You are, indeed, correct. The text is "the strength of the line facing the Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: "... and facing the BH Army." And then, sir: "Our aim is to create a situation in which the Muslims will not trust one another, which will make them easy to control."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My only question to you on this document, sir, is: Isn't this -- doesn't this describe the attitude of the HVO towards the Bregava Brigade throughout? They were trying to neutralise them, as such, in all their actions since they were created; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document indicates -- or, rather, shows the opinion of an officer of the Security Service, how he views the situation. Now, I really don't know how that Security Service worked, so that many of the things written down here are ones that I can't confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But my question remains. Wasn't it the basic premise of the HVO, then, looking at those words, to at least control or neutralise, then, the Bregava Brigade in Stolac? Would you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we talked about the efforts made by the Bregava Brigade throughout our discussions here, and it's quite normal that if you know that somebody is going to attack you imminently, that you have to prepare for the attack and prepare for your defence. And what I see here is that this particular person was preparing facts and information gathered by his service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's look at the document just previous to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor is putting a question to you, but there is part of a document that he did not mention, and I believe that it was a very important part. If a reasonable Judge looks at the transcript without looking at the document, he might make a mistake. And why is it? Well, the Prosecutor is using this document because he believes that it's a genuine document, since he's using them, and in this document I see that Pavlovic -- Zarko Pavlovic is saying that the HVO arrested 183 ABiH soldiers, and by looking at the documentation in the archives, there was confirmation of the fact that the estimation made earlier by the superiors was correct, because the Bregava Brigade had indeed prepared an operation in order to occupy the area of responsibility of the 1st Knez Domagoj Brigade. So according to this document, which is used by the Prosecutor and which has probative value in the eyes of the OTP, it seems that the arrest of these 183 soldiers was linked to a preventive action, because the ABiH intended to later occupy the area of responsibility. And so the potential aggressor was not the HVO, but the ABiH. Now, you were on the ground, so is that what you experienced, i.e., that 183 of your fellow Muslim soldiers had been arrested, but they'd been arrested because they were plotting an action against the HVO? Is this what this document is actually saying or, according to the Prosecution's version, is it because -- did you arrest them because that was in line with the ultimatum made by Mate Boban and this had nothing to do with the action that was being planned by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's precisely as you described it. That's what I'm saying. That's how I claim it was. They had to be disarmed as a preventive measure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before the break, if I may ask just one more question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, in light of your earlier evidence, however, where you said that the Bregava Brigade was not strong, and as it was also mentioned by Judge Trechsel - I don't know if those were the precise words - but they were pretty much worthless, according to your evidence, so any assertion that they would try to take over the zone of responsibility and -- from the Knez Domagoj Brigade or take on the Knez Domagoj Brigade, according to your own evidence, that would be a laughable proposition; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it's not a laughable proposition at all, because they took over the area of responsibility beforehand and lost it, so these were irresponsible soldiers. And most probably they would have taken over our zone of responsibility, but what would have happened to the zone is something we can only speculate about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one further document on this topic, and do we have time? It's a brief document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, finish with it. It's better to finalise this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if we could quickly look - I think it's two documents earlier in your binder, and that is document P02640, P02640. Yes, you have that document.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this document, if I look at it, it is a document by yourself. Is that your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You shake your head. Is that a Yes?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is a document dated 5 June 1993 to the military police in Stolac. "Subject: Search warrant." "This warrants the search of homes and property of the following HVO members. All weaponry and military equipment found is to be confiscated, saved that belonging to the HVO." And then following -- 28 names follow. Is this indeed a document prepared by you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The names of these 27 [sic] people, looking through them quickly, these are all people of Muslim ethnicity; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you mentioned that prior to the attack on the 30th of June on the North Camp, you were totally surprised, that you had no indication previously that such an event could occur. In light of that, isn't this an indication that actually you were suspicious of Muslims even before that time? This is three weeks before that period.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I wrote this document myself, I know what it's about. None of these soldiers here was taken into detention. We, for security reasons, searched them, searched the hamlet, or village, whichever you like, and it was the village of Borojevici, in fact, because we had received certain information telling us that at that time, in that particular village, there were people coming in who had a destructive effect and that they were members of the BH Army, that they were passing through the village or spent time in the village, and that, anyway, in that particular village weapons and ammunition were being hidden. And so we had to take this kind of action. And as you can see here in the last five words of the introduction, it says "military equipment should be confiscated, except for that issued by the Croatian Defence Council and belonging to the HVO." So our soldiers were not under threat in any way, and we acted properly towards them to the very last day, in the way that I have described during my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that it was actions such as this, aimed at Muslims in Stolac, which raised the tension and the fears of the Muslims that they were being targeted by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can tell you is what I know, which is that none of these people protested, and there was no fear, except in individual cases, except in individual cases. Yes, certain individuals, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: My final question, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, there's something I can't understand. The order you signed seems to be very kind, because should these soldiers have materiel that they acquired illegally, for instance, military equipment that they were not supposed to have, well, you should have ordered for them to be arrested. But here, you're not saying that they should be arrested. And you even add in this document that if they have equipment belonging to the HVO, they should keep it. So I don't understand. This document is used by the Prosecutor in support of its case, and if you look at the document from a purely military point of view, I think that this is very kind towards these soldiers, who could be offenders because they have weapons that they acquired under apparently illegal circumstances. So why didn't you demand them to be arrested in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, until you find something in somebody's possession, you cannot charge him with anything. So if we had found something here, we would have taken appropriate measures. But ordering our soldiers to take measures against them, without knowing that they had actually offended, was certainly nothing that we wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully agree with you, Witness. But why did you fail to say the following: If equipment that was acquired illegally is discovered, arrest the people holding them, draft an indictment, and pass it on to the military prosecutor? Why did you not say that in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to the report received from the unit that carried out this task, I would have ordered such measures. But as far as I remember, to my recollection, nothing was found on that occasion, apart from materiel issued by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. -- sorry. Mr. Pavlovic, on a legal level, what you ordered was a measure that's normally in the hands of the judiciary because it's an interference with a fundamental right; protection of home. On what did you base your authority to take such an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I based it on intelligence that I received, because I must act in a preventive fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I mean, you are not a lawyer. I will not insist, but intelligence is certainly not a legal basis to interfere with fundamental rights. On the opposite, fundamental rights are protected formally. But I will not insist. You are not a lawyer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, be quick because we should have a break. If the other Trial Chamber had not taken six more minutes, we would have been done by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The last question. Number 9 on the list, Mr. Mustafa Obradovic, is that the Mustafa Obradovic who was later killed in Gabela Prison; do you know?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know the man personally, nor do I know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the next exhibit that I'd like to refer you to is Exhibit P08637. Your binder's already open at the document. P08637. And, sir, this document is a Security and Information Service's report of 8 January 1996, and the report is -- and I'll read the first bit: "We submit to you the list of HVO military commanders (with their personal data) who were performing their duties during the mass exile of Bosnian Muslims from the region of Stolac." And then number 1 refers to: "Bozo Pavlovic, son of Ante, born 24 October 1966 ..." And that's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And it says that: "At the above-mentioned time, he was the commander of defence of the town of Stolac. At the end of June he was replaced by Veseljko Raguz. Still, he remained there and he was present during the exile and while arrests were carried out." Is that correct, accurate?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, from the documents that we have seen so far it is plain to see how long I was at Stolac and what my duties were there. I cannot accept this kind of assessment, the assessment of the author of this document. I cannot accept it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, he refers to "exile," he uses the word in B/C/S I see it's "progona." You wouldn't disagree with a statement that Muslims were removed from Stolac municipality and that -- and to use his word, this exile, that it was affected by the HVO? Would you disagree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I cannot prevent the author of this document from calling it whatever he pleases, but I can say that these last words after the comma are false, because I wasn't in the area at that time at all, and it can be seen from other documents where I really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, but aside from where you were at that period, is it correct that the HVO exiled the Muslims from Stolac, the Muslim inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find the right word for this qualification because I do not know what happened there at the time. How the Muslim people left the area of Stolac isn't anything that I can confirm. I can only relate rumours that reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, three months after July 1993, in September 1993, do you know that Andjelko Markovic informed President Tudjman that not a single Muslim remained in Stolac? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've only heard it from you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Before stepping off this document, number 33, right at the end of the document, is a reference to Mr. Andjelko Markovic, and it says he is a doctor by profession and he worked in the orthopaedic hospital in Stolac at the time. That orthopaedic hospital in Stolac, is that the "kostana" hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the start of the war, as far as I know, because I didn't live in the area of Stolac then, but I know that Mr. Markovic is a medical doctor. And as far as I know, until the beginning of the war, he worked at the "kostana" hospital, the bone hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, obviously back in January 1996, following the Dayton Agreements or Accords, there were investigations that were carried out to find out who did what, and here we have 33 individuals being listed who may have played a part with relation to the issue of Muslims in Stolac, and you are under number 1. Therefore, as far as you know, in 1996 or thereafter were you called by the police services to be interviewed as to your possible part or were you never called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I state under oath that this is the first time anybody has asked me to speak about these things. I have never been interviewed by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that you already answered the next question I was going to ask you, but I still ask it for the record. In the following years up to today, were you ever called or interviewed by the OTP or were you never asked anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no service either in or outside Bosnia-Herzegovina has ever demanded that I give any kind of statement about wartime events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At least this is a very clear answer. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there is a document in evidence, and I'm -- it's in the binder, but I'm not going to let you look at it. I'll simply refer you to what's in the document and then go on from there. The document I'm referring to, for the record, is P02215. It's already in evidence. And, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Why shouldn't the witness be allowed to look at the document? I mean, because he may be taking something out of context. I find this rather incredible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Mr. Kruger, sorry, why don't you want the witness to see the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a simple question of time economics, that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. But just say, well, you have the document, and then you can ask your question. If he wants to look at the document, he can. But at any rate, the Judges check everything. Rest assured, nothing will escape my notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the document I'm referring to was an order by Mr. Nedjeljko Obradovic on 7 May 1993, and it contained the following segment, which was bullet number 13, and it said: "The commander of the Stolac Forward Command Post shall immediately block admission of new patients into the osteopathic hospital and the taking out of material and technical equipment from it." My question to you, sir: Did you ever receive an order with regard to the "kostana" hospital in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could be shown the second page of the document, because I can only see items 1 through 7 and you were referring to item 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The document, if we -- there, it's on your screen now, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's number 13.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I received this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, the patients in the osteopathic hospital or the "kostana" hospital, were they also removed from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, at that time, the time when I arrived at Stolac, I cannot claim to be precise, but I'm sure that there weren't even ten patients in that hospital. And when this order was drafted, there are statements about there being over a hundred patients in the hospital, and the commander of the brigade ordered me to provide security to that hospital and to prevent them from taking in new patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, something is not clear in my mind. It may be a problem due to translation. I understand that you say that there were 10 seats and that there were 100 patients, because in the English version it looks like there are 10 patients and then 100. So what did you mean to say? Did you mean to say that there were only 10 beds and then that there were 100 people, so you could not admit everybody? So what did you mean to say, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Here's what I said: When I took over my duty at Stolac in July 1993, there were -- don't take my word for it, but fewer than 10 patients in the hospital. And at the time when this order was drafted, the hospital had over a hundred patients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, now it's clear. Now I understand, because when you took over the command, there were only 10 patients, and when Obradovic issued that order in May, there were 100 patients. Fine, everything's clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I'd like to refer you to the next document, and it's towards the end of the binder, Exhibit P11098. And if I may state up front, Your Honour, it's a new document and it's being shown to the witness as a matter of credibility. 11098. Now, sir, this document is an ECMM report from the legal adviser, and the subject is: "A possible war crime." And it's dated 2 June 1993, and it says: "In Stolac," the second paragraph: "In Stolac, on 9 May 1993, HVO captured the orthopaedic centre, threw out about 100 people, some seriously ill, and the rest of the following doctors and nurses from the staff: Dr. Mehmet Kadic, Mustafa Pasarla [phoen], Dinka Seta," et cetera, et cetera, and then it says: "The suspected perpetrator is supposed to be commander of Stolac HVO, Commander Bozo Pavlovic." Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, my fellow Judge draws my attention to something which is quite right. You're a witness, so you answer questions. But at your level, if you feel that the answer might incriminate you - one never knows - you can say that you don't want to answer, and if he insists, he has to go through the Trial Chamber, and based on the Rules the Trial Chamber may grant you immunity, if you are of the view that in answering the question, you might incriminate yourself. Well, I don't know, but you have to see for yourself. This is something I was bound to tell you. I know it's quite a complex rule, and I thank my fellow Judge for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And so, Witness, are you prepared to give us an answer to that? Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you going to put to me a question or do you just want my opinion on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you know about the fact that you were, in some circles, being viewed as a potential war criminal?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, I can tell now, only having seen these documents. I didn't know it at the time. But I can explain. Here, I have said that when I came to Stolac, there were fewer than 10 patients in the hospital. They were seriously ill, with disabilities, and they were there when the war started. It was an osteopathic hospital, one of the best known of its kind in all of the former Yugoslavia. There were some patients from Serbia and other faraway places, and their families were unable to evacuate them, so the situation came about that the hospital management and the hospital staff started collecting old women from the streets of Stolac and taking them to the hospital because they wanted to receive humanitarian aid on account of that, and the international community indeed provided such aid in large quantities. It is very important that I finish, if you allow me. On one occasion, I don't exactly recall the name of the gentleman, but he was an EC monitor, he called at my headquarters frequently and then he would continue to the hospital, and I received information that the director of the hospital, Dr. Kapic, was putting forward very serious accusations against me and the HVO, even though I was in good relations with him at the time and now, nowadays too. And when that gentleman from the international community came the next time, I expressed my desire to go to the hospital with him, and we sat down with Dr. Kapic together. After the informal introductory conversation, the gentleman from the international community asked me to leave him to speak to Dr. Kapic in four hours, and I said, No problem, but I would like to ask a few questions of the doctor before I leave you. And then I did so, because I had heard that we were treating the patients badly, and I asked him whether our command had offered him to provide food to the hospital, fuel for the ambulances, and all other provisions that our services had, and the doctor answered in the affirmative. I asked him whether there had been any problems between us, and he answered in the negative. And I asked him how much food he was receiving for the hospital - this is very important - and where that food was ending up, and how many meals the patients were receiving, because I had information that the patients were only receiving two meals, but there was food for four meals, and there was much fuel for the hospital, but the radiators in the hospital were cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I'm afraid I have to move on. Our time is running out. What I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask just one small question. Can you approximately give a date of that visit of yours to the "kostana" hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you the exact date, but I know that it was in spring 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I would like to point out something. Since the same document under number P02612 is under seal, this should be considered to prevent possible problems in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Did you know that it was a document under seal? I asked myself that question, but you seem to be so confident that I thought I must have been wrong about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can just check my situation for a moment. I think I have the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, Witness, based on this document, well, the source is the (redacted) (redacted). He mentioned -- he reported the event. When you were on the ground, did you have any contacts with SpaBat, and with this captain in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a SpaBat in our area, but I don't remember any individual by name. I probably wouldn't recognise anyone if I were to see one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But there's a minor problem. This operation apparently took place on the 9th of May in the hospital, and we know that there were some events that took place in Mostar on that same date. It may be a mere coincidence, but as far as you know, as far as you can remember, but this may be a difficult question, was there an overall plan by the HVO on the 9th of May to take control of positions held by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know of any such plans.
