utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, just to respond, the first part of the document which is being shown outside the courtroom is, indeed, not under seal. The second part of the document, which essentially says the same, is under seal and shouldn't have been included in the binder. That is my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just to conclude on this topic: You won't dispute that the Muslim patients who were held in -- who were in "kostana" hospital ended up in the Grabovina Barracks and from there they were ultimately expelled to ABiH territory at a time later. You don't dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an objection to the fact that he said Muslim patients. We haven't made that distinction yet. All we spoke about was patients in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sustained. I was going to make the same observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, the patients in the "kostana" hospital, those who couldn't be taken by their families, they ended up in Grabovina Barracks in Capljina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that is partially correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, there's evidence before the Chamber by a person who drove a truck a while later with patients on the back of that truck from -- turned out to be from the "kostana" hospital and who were taken to ABiH territory. You won't dispute that that happened to certain of those patients?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to object once again. The question doesn't contain the time that the Prosecutor is referring to. I know the time-frame that the witness mentioned, but the fact is: Was this witness there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm simply putting to the witness that he doesn't dispute that that ultimately happened to these patients, and it was a matter of two or three months after they were taken to Grabovina Barracks, if that long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, as far as I remember, in that hospital the real patients that were unable to move, and that's what the hospital was basically used for, incapacitated patients, they were mostly of Serb ethnicity. Now, all the others, up to a hundred of them, were people who were able to move around and they didn't need to be hospitalised. Now, the Serb patients there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I may, but do you -- do you dispute that fact or don't you, or don't you know what happened? Whether that's true or not, my question.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time-frame does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This would have been in June 1993, 'round about June 1993, perhaps early July.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could not have happened in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And in July?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for July, I can't say anything about that because I wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's step on to another topic, which I will touch upon very briefly. I'm going to refer you to a Defence document that was shown to you, and we'll just look at it on the screen. It's 4D02000. It's not in that binder. 4D02000. And you will recall this was the letter by Mr. Markovic and yourself to Mr. Boban on the 22nd of May, 1993. You recall that, that letter? It's --

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the letter that I see in front of me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, I'm just going to refer to one part of that letter, and it's on the second page in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, so you can work correctly and so you don't waste time, let me tell you that you have just 30 minutes left, 3-0, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At the beginning -- or close to the top of the second page, it says: "During the Serbian aggression, almost all Catholic places of worship were destroyed, and not a single Islamic place of worship was seriously damaged. Since the liberation of Stolac, there has been no destruction of Islamic religious buildings, apart from that caused by Serbian artillery attacks." Sir, that's correct, at least on the 22nd of May, 1993, all the mosques in Stolac were still standing?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an authentic letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And if we say "all the mosques in Stolac," would that also include the mosques throughout the municipality and not only those in the town of Stolac?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I think the answer to that would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, early in July, when you were still the commander of the Stolac defence, were all those mosques and Islamic religious buildings still standing?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until my departure, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, you are aware, coming from Stolac, that the town of Stolac had an old Turkish market in the center of town, surrounding the Sultan Selim Mosque; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And that was also still standing at the time that you left Stolac early in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, is it also correct that shortly afterwards, all four of the mosques in the town of Stolac as well as the entire Turkish old market at the Tepa [phoen] was totally obliterated and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 200 per cent, yes. I think they all were, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you disagree --

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- two -- I'm certain that two were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you disagree -- or you can't disagree that it was -- the destruction that took place that we're talking about now was caused or perpetrated by members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't know who the perpetrators of those crimes were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And at the time when you left, in the town of Stolac there was no fighting; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no street-fighting, but there could have been shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on to my final topic, which deals with forced labour. And if I can very briefly refer you, just to set the tone, to Exhibit P01765, P01765, and it's about six or -- seven or eight documents into your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I'd like to have it down on the record that we're entering a new area which wasn't contained in the examination-in-chief, so I'd just like the Trial Chamber to rule on whether or not they're going to permit Mr. Kruger to broach a new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, this is a new topic. Why do you want to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, it's a very relevant topic, that the documents that will be shown to the witness in this regard are documents which many of them bear his name, so he was intimately involved in the whole process, and I think from that point of view he can really assist the Chamber in understanding the issue of forced labour, insofar as he was involved in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, because this issue has come up before, and in anticipation of that I even brought the Federal Rules of evidence from the United States, Rule 611(B) is the one that this rule has been inspired by this Tribunal -- this Trial Chamber and others, it says: "Scope of cross-examination. Cross-examination should be limited to the subject matter of the direct examination and matters affecting the credibility of the witness. The Court may, in the exercise of discretion, permit inquiry into additional matters as if on direct examination." That's Rule 611(B), and that's what has been applied against the Defence, and so I do think that this is a matter that is outside the scope of cross-examination. I leave it to your discretion to determine to what extent this matter fits within the credibility of the witness. But from what I understand from Mr. Kruger, he sees these documents as being interesting for the Trial Chamber and not for the credibility of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult with my fellow Judges and ask them whether they allow for these questions to be put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, you may put the questions to the witness, notably since we have a document where there is mention of his name. So I'm sure he will tell us why his name is on the document and why prisoners had to go and work. It might be interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have the document there. This is the stamped log-book of approvals for engagement of detainees and work from 2 April 1993 to 8 March 1994, and it is in evidence. I'd like to refer you to line 82 in the document, entry 82. Do you have that? And it says: "Request for taking 10 detainees needed for work, 10 August 1993." Reference number: "Third Brigade, Bozo Pavlovic." Is it correct, sir, that you authorised people to take detainees for labour, members from your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is a request probably signed by me, and those detainees most probably went to work, but I can't see where; perhaps in the barracks somewhere or something like that, because when I leafed through it, through these documents briefly, I see that there are another couple of people from the 3rd Brigade that are mentioned here. For example, Ivica Matinovic, and that was a gentleman who at that time was in charge of the Quarter-Master Service, and probably they needed a warehouse somewhere, or a kitchen perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I've gone through this document, and I've found entries similar to this one in line 94, line 103, line 104, line 148, line 199, and then entries from number 223 to 232. For time take, I'll refer you to entry 230, line 230. You have that towards the end, and it says: "Request for taking 10 detainees needed for work." Again: "Bozo Pavlovic." It's 21 of July. That's the day after you assumed command of the 3rd Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, is it safe to say that for the three months that you were in the command, or was it -- from July to October, throughout that whole period you authorised members of your unit to take detainees for forced labour, or labour, at least?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the members of the 3rd Brigade unit at that time on a daily basis used detainees or prisoners in order to perform the daily jobs and work that had to be done on the territory of the 3rd Brigade. And I wish to stress here that the 3rd Brigade itself at that time was holding positions behind which there were many military facilities which were left over from the Yugoslav People's Army. We had to maintain those facilities and use them. The Heliodrom complex, for example, was a vast military facility, and life went on, on a daily basis, quite normally there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you and refer you to a related topic, then. Is it correct that detainees escaped at times while performing labour for members of your unit? And for this I'll refer you to Exhibit P03788. It's about 10 documents on in your binder, P03788. Now, sir, the document is from Mr. Stanko Bozic, the warden at Heliodrom. It's dated 29 July 1993, and it's a report sent to Mr. Coric, Mr. Mijo Jelic, Zvonko Vidovic, and yourself, Mr. Bozo Pavlovic. It says: "28 July, the request of 24 July from 3rd Brigade relating to work until further notice, signed by Brigadier Bozo Pavlovic. The request was satisfied." And then there's a report that a detainee, Ahmet Trbonja, was not brought back, and the aforementioned soldier explained that he had escaped while working at the Buna work site. Very briefly, sir, the Buna work site, was that on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as I remember, that could only have been about people working on the bridge that was being built across the Neretva River, in the settlement of Buna. The bridge was shielded by a hill, which is the start of Gubavica, and it's away from the front-line at a distance of two to three kilometres, in fact, from the front-line, and so those detainees were not under any threat at all, working in the area. The bridge was under intensive construction at the time, and construction work went on for several months. Now, you asked me before that whether there were cases where the detainees fled, tried to escape. There were lots of cases like that, because the relationship of the people in our unit towards these others, people working together with them, was really a little strange, because they didn't feel themselves to be prisoners at all. I would come by and see them all sitting down together, drinking, on that same bridge, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I have a number of other documents which also are similar to this one in showing that detainees had escaped, but let's turn it up a step and see about detainees being wounded. And for this, I'm going to show you a new document, and this does relate to credibility, and it is Exhibit P11094. It's towards the end of your binder, P11094. You have the document. Once again, it's an official note dated 24 July. It's from Mr. Stanko Bozic, warden of the Heliodrom Remand Prison, and it's addressed to Mr. Coric, Josip Dodik, and to you, Mr. Bozo Pavlovic. It says 22 July, on the basis of a request, once again by the HVO 3rd Brigade, "prisoners were provided for work at the Buna Bridge. Mr. Mate Baric took charge of the detainees. They were returned from work with a statement that detainee Hasan Becirovic was missing, having been wounded by BH Army and transferred to Metkovic hospital for treatment." Sir, did you know or were you aware of this instance where a detainee had been wounded while performing labour?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was two days after I took up my duties, but this is the first time that I see this document. I've never seen it before, and I don't know that this person was wounded. But quite possibly he was wounded by an enemy shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that -- I can't show them all to you, due to time constraints. I have a number of other documents similar to this indicating detainees being wounded while performing labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned friend will no doubt forgive me. Before he puts his next question, may I once again seek the assistance of the Court Officer to request technical assistance? Once again, it seems that gremlins have bedevilled the LiveNote transcript of the Defence, and perhaps somebody could come into court to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar is going to take care of this. Witness, you didn't come here to talk about forced labour, but my question is going to go to the crux of the problem. As far as you know, were detainees forced to work on the front-line or, according to you, were they sent to do other kind of work, like bridges or kitchen duty? In 394 [as interpreted], you'd asked for two women. I guess that was for kitchen duty. So according to you, were these prisoners placed on the front-line to dig the trenches and to fortify the front-line or were they sent elsewhere to do other kind of jobs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am speaking about the time that I spent in the 3rd Brigade, and during that time the prisoners, who were mostly from our unit who were disarmed, they worked on facilities and features such as the kitchen. At least 10 or 15 people worked in the kitchens on a daily basis, and in the washer rooms. They cleaned the premises. They worked in the warehouses and in the various craft shops. They maintained roads, built bridges. And that's all that I can remember for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There's a mistake on the transcript. Line 16, it wasn't "394," but "94." It was number 94. In entry 94, there is a request for two women. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this exhibit that we're looking at was also sent to Mr. Coric. Did you hear anything from Mr. Coric in regard to this? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object. This is a new document, and as Mr. Kruger previously said -- well, this isn't a question related to the credibility of this witness, but it has to do with Mr. Coric, himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber granted leave to the Prosecution to put questions, and there is a document that was addressed to Mr. Coric, as I can see. So that's all. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, did you hear anything from Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kruger. I do not quite see how this can help the Chamber to evaluate the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I'll need to refer you to a different document which has the same bearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like an answer from the Prosecutor, because he must demonstrate that the gentleman indicated one answer and now he is trying to confront him and challenge the credibility. That's how it's done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think he took my point and is going to another document and is abandoning that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, we must all listen sharply, but we cannot always listen with full sharpness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll refer you to document 3939, P03939.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it toward the end or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: It's more to the beginning, about a third of the way into the binder, sir. This is a document which is, indeed, in evidence.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3939, but I can't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may ask the assistance of the usher, please. Your Honour, if I may inform the Court at this stage, after this document there are only two exhibits that I would still wish to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, so that you don't get lost or drowned in all these documents, you're now pointing to a document, but there is another one, number 3788. It's the same document, but with a different date. This is a report by Mr. Bozic, the warden of the military prison, who sends his report to Mr. Coric, Mr. Pavlovic, and another two individuals. So it could be that the witness does not know that this report was sent to Mr. Coric, so bear this in mind when putting your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, this document is 4 August 1993, signed by Stanko Bozic, and it's addressed -- sent to Mr. Coric, Mr. Jelic, and to you, Mr. Bozo Pavlovic. And it says: "3 August, request from Mr. Bozo Pavlovic ..." So once again labour approved by you. It says: "When the group returned from work, they were all covered in blood and beaten up. Three of them had sustained grave injuries. The reason given was that they had attempted to escape." And the Central Military Remand Prison was not happy about this. They say: "... for the sake of its function and repute, these matters shall no longer be tolerated." Now, sir, from this, it would appear that this is a clear case where a crime has been committed, prisoners had been beaten up. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this particular instance. I can explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may ask you, sir, did you hear anything from Mr. Coric or from the military police in regard to this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why do you want to intervene, Mr. Coric? The witness is at the stand. He's the witness. If you intervene, you may prompt his answer, so I fail to understand. Why are you up? Well, now that you're on your feet, you can speak. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] I will not go into the usual practice here to suggest an answer to the witness, but I would like to ask the Prosecutor to provide a basis for this question. I'm not objecting to this question, but it would be logical to ask Mr. Pavlovic whether we were in the same command line, whether we had any contacts, whether we had had any contacts, whether any one of us was superior to the other. That was all I wanted to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but I thought that the witness was about to answer because he wanted to provide an answer; that's all the more reason. The Prosecutor asked you something. You wanted to answer, and then we had Mr. Coric, who explained what the problem was about. Now please answer the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was going to reply along the same lines as what Mr. Coric said. Mr. Coric and I had practically no contacts throughout the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, apart from meeting each other at some celebrations or festive occasions. That's where I -- that's how I know him, and those were our contacts after the war, too. So Mr. Coric and I never spoke about these events, if this is indeed an answer to your question, if I understood your question well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm afraid I'd like to explore it further, but in the view of time, I am going to move on, ask you one question and then show two documents. The further question: We've seen that detainees were wounded while on labour. Is it also correct that there were detainees who were killed while performing labour?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, in the zone of responsibility of my brigade no one detainee was killed while performing labour. And I said a short while ago that I can explain this instance and that I gave orders to launch proceedings against the perpetrators of this crime. And that was the only thing I could do, because this wasn't even a unit of the 3rd Brigade. It was a unit of the Siroki Brijeg Anti-Aircraft Defence, and I remember the situation. On that day, a soldier from that unit heard that his brother had been killed, and he started mistreating a detainee, but I remember that the commander of that unit was ordered to launch an inquiry against that soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, earlier on, in that document where mention was made of the 30 soldiers building the bridge, I noticed that they were guarded by one soldier, whose name we have, but I also noted that this was not a soldier from your unit. He was a soldier from the 7th Brigade. So how is it that you could require prisoners and that they were being guarded by other soldiers? Was that something normal, militarily speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm back to the document in question. Here, this is about a soldier from the 7th Battalion, and it belonged to the 3rd Brigade. We had -- well, the names that were used were a bit odd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, 7th Battalion, not 7th Brigade. Sorry for this. Mr. Kruger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, let's very briefly look at your authority. Where did you derive your authority to authorise labour by detainees? And for this, if you can look, it's a few documents earlier in your binder, Exhibit P03592, P03592. This exhibit is already in evidence, and this is an order -- I'll wait for you. 3592. Mr. Usher, if I could impose on you, please.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 3592, is that the document you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: 3592, that's correct. Sir, if you see, this is a written -- handwritten document, but if we look at the document which purports to be by General Petkovic, it's dated 20 July 1993, and it says: "In view of the fact that the last order to conduct engineering work is not being observed, I hereby warn for the last time and order:" And then it says, number 3: "Continue to fortify all positions." 4 is: "Engage the prisoners and available machinery in the completion of this task," so "engage the prisoners." Sir, this 20 July is the day that you assumed command of the 3rd Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, is it correct to say that your authority to authorise the taking of detainees for labour actually derives directly from your superior commander, Mr. Milivoj Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, to my mind this can be a coincidence, I mean the matching dates. But as far as I remember, upon my arrival at the 3rd Brigade, it had already been common practice for soldiers -- detainees, disarmed soldiers from our brigade and other brigades, other brigades of the HVO, can be used for chores that I have already mentioned, and there were many such chores. And I merely continued the existing practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's look at the very last document that I'm going to show you, and it is Exhibit P05873, 5873.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this, once again, is a document by Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, dated 14 October 1993, and that's the time you were handing over the 3rd Brigade Command to your successor, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And this order says: "I order -- I hereby prohibit the removal of prisoners to perform any kind of labour in the brigades' respective zones of responsibility." "Should such activity nevertheless be allowed, the permit shall be issued by the HVO Main Staff." Sir, so I put it to you again that the authority that you had exercised previously, and subsequent to this, to authorise detainees being taken for labour, that authority was derived from General Petkovic in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I repeat once more that I cannot agree with this qualification. This is merely a numeric coincidence. But I claim that I took over the brigade -- the command of the brigade on the 20th of July and continued existing practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, that wasn't translated. I have two minutes? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, my last question to you: On this issue of detainees, during your months as commander of the 3rd Brigade, detainees had appeared -- I'm referring to labour authorised by you. Detainees had appeared -- detainees were wounded, injured, and I put it to you that there is also actually one report of a detainee being killed. But the point I want to ask you about is: Did you report -- in your hand, ever report to your successor that there were problems with labour and that he should be very careful?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as I remember, there is a complete protocol on the hand-over of duty in which it is recorded that I acquainted my successor with all the problems in the brigade and on the territory where I was, and that I was at his disposal for 10 days subsequently. And I believe that I gave him good information about everything and enabled him to discharge his duty in a good fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I regret we cannot continue our discussion. I would have liked to do so, but thank you very much. And no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. We're doing redirect. Ms. Alaburic, how long do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Your Honours. Good evening to everybody in the courtroom. I announced the redirect examination for Mr. Pavlovic in the duration of, I think, an hour and a half. I will do my utmost, although two very important new topics have been opened during the cross-examination, but I will try to finish today. I will start with my redirect examination where the Prosecutor broke off, and that is the labour of detainees. And the Prosecutor's assertion that General Petkovic, with some orders of his, actually opened the gates to lower-level commanders to use detained persons for some types of labour or work assignments. I would also like to thank my learned friend Mr. Kruger who was careful to be consistent in the use of "detainees" throughout his cross-examination, which will help us to finish off this topic rather soon with you, Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have received the entire set of documents, I would ask you to look at two separate documents, P514, 514. I'll repeat, P514. That is correct. It is -- it's an instruction for the operation of the Central Military Prison in Mostar. Let us immediately turn to page 5 in the Croatian original, and it's page 8 in the English translation. We see here, under items 1 and 2, the definitions of two categories of imprisoned persons. Item 1 defines the notion of prisoners of war, and item 2 deals with the definition of military prisoners, or military detainees, in the words of Defence counsel. Tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, once a soldier of the ABiH is imprisoned, to which category of these two does he belong?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier of the ABiH is considered a prisoner of war, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so item 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you imprison a soldier of the HVO on whichever grounds, into which category does that soldier fall of these two?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I imprison a soldier from my unit, then he is considered a detainee; that is, he falls under item 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In all your documents that my learned friend has showed you, if I read correctly, the word "detainee" is consistently used; am I right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, to who did those labour orders of yours apply?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember having mentioned that already. The facilities I mentioned -- at the facilities I mentioned, the people who worked were the disarmed members of our brigade, that is, the 3rd, and other brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So they were HVO soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the following document, P6805, 6805. And under item 1 of this document, we can read -- sorry, item 5: "It was decreed that prisoners could be used for work (arranging the terrain) with the signature of the commander of the Military Police Battalion, or the brigade, with the mandatory submission," I can't read a word, "and a report after the return." You told us, Mr. Pavlovic, that before you commanded the 3rd Brigade, it had already been practice for detained persons to be sent to carry out some kinds of work?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I can give you a specific instance. On the 20th of July, when I took over the command of the brigade, the first thing I did was visit the workshop and the kitchen, and I saw detainees working there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to these documents - I have no time now to read out the documents in their entirety - it was clearly described that prisoners of war are to be treated in accordance with the Geneva Conventions; in other words, that they must not to be sent to the front-line to perform work or be used for military purposes. Were you acquainted with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And just one more question about this topic. If you were to approach the prison director to give you a number of detained persons to carry out some work, who was it that selected the persons to carry out that work as requested by you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly do not know who decided on who was to go. Somebody from the prison. But I know that after a certain time, those who had filed a request would ask to be given the same men again because they had, in the meantime, become friends or at least they were known persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's return to this larger set of documents. The Prlic Defence showed you document 1D1704. That is a document by which Mate Boban's order, dated 15th of September, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat these last words?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This order is forwarded to all units of the Zone of Operations North-West Herzegovina. And the second document is 4D1067, 1067, with which the same order is forwarded to all units of the Zone of Operations of South-East Herzegovina. Please take a look at the third document in this set. This is Mate Boban's order dated 15 September 1993, and the document number is P5104, 5104. If you look at items 1 and 2 of this order, Mr. Pavlovic, is there any doubt, to your mind, that these two items referred to the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I just re-emphasise the point to my learned friend. Of course, she is very experienced and is aware of it. Re-examination, of course, is not a license to lead, and I would ask that she ensure that non-leading questions are asked, and notwithstanding the fact that ostensibly this re-examination arises out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, please rephrase your question, and be more careful in rephrasing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I'm grateful for this suggestion. I will do so. I thought this was notorious, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, take a look at the -- to the distribution list to who this order was forwarded.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Defence Department, the Main Staff of the Armed Forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and the files.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the following document, P4275. These are the minutes taken at a working meeting convened on the 18th of August, 1993, in the -- on the premises of the HVO HZ-HB. Mr. Pavlovic, please take a look at the list of persons present. Was the commander of the Main Staff there, his deputy, or anyone from the Main Staff or any unit of the Army of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see no familiar name from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please look at the following page under Roman numeral II. Conclusions are being listed, and please read to us item 3.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Defence Department, the Department of Justice and General Administration are charged with undertaking measures and activities relating to organising military prisons and adequate capacity to accommodate prisoners of war, in accordance with international conventions."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, if you cast an eye on this document, is any task issued to the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that I was able to read it out in this short time, no, I wouldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the following document, P4841. These are the minutes of the working meeting of the Cabinet of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, held on the 6th of September, 1993. Please take a look at the list of persons present. Mr. Pavlovic, is any of these persons from the Main Staff or any military unit of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know all these persons, but those I know are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please read out to us Conclusion number 1.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Determine locations for the detention of prisoners of war. Adopt regulations on the conditions and procedure for the detention of prisoners of war at centres for prisoners of war, which must be founded on the provisions of International Law of War. Bring the conditions in the current centres to the required level with maximum observation of the regulations of International Law of War, International Humanitarian Law, and other regulations mentioned above. Secure equipment and materiel, and appoint staff to run the administrative services at centres for prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, please read out to us Conclusion number 3.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In order to improve the conditions of accommodation and diet of detainees, the Office for Expelled Persons, Refugees, and Displaced Persons is tasked to ensure the necessary qualities of food, personal hygiene items, and, if possible," or, "to the extent possible, equipment and materiel needed for accommodation (blankets, mats, et cetera)."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you have now read out almost the entire document. Was the Main Staff of the HVO given any task with relation to these detention centres for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That doesn't follow from anything I have read.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at the following document, please, P5264. I don't know whether it's been up-loaded to e-court. If it has, we can continue. It's a report of a French news agency about Bosnian Croats to close Dretelj prison camp. It says: "Bosnian Croat authorities, on Tuesday, are to close down the Dretelj prison camp in Southern Bosnia, where more than 500 Muslims are being held. The 'prime minister' of," now I quote, "the self-declared Bosnian Croat republic said --" they're referring to Mr. Jadranko Prlic, and the document goes on to read that: "The dead-line for closing Dretelj is Tuesday afternoon, and that dead-line was agreed between leaders of the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian leaders for the bilateral and unconditional dismantling of all prison camps." My question to you, Mr. Pavlovic, is: Did you know that Dretelj prison was closed down at a certain time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was closed down. But when, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Pavlovic, to the questions of Mr. Coric's Defence, you spoke partly about activities under documents that were sent to the 3rd Battalion, or let us proceed upward, the 3rd Platoon of the 3rd Company of the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police. The question is recorded on page 22 of yesterday's transcript; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, was that the brigade military police or the military police? The brigade police or active military police?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've just said now, it was the active military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, who was the commander of that 3rd Military Police Battalion at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who the commander of the platoon and company was, but I can't remember who the commander of the battalion was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And do you know who was the immediate superior to the commander of the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police had its own establishment and it's chain of -- vertical chain of command, but I really can't say what that was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the chief of the Military Police Administration was at that time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the administration was Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's now look at the documents we've already discussed once again. And the first of those is P1913, which is a request from the Command of the 1st Brigade of the HVO, and the second document is P1900, and that is an order of roughly the same contents, issued on the same day by the same person. Now, can you, Mr. Pavlovic, tell us why one of these documents is called "Request" and the other is called "Order"?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, they were drafted on the same day, and I really don't know what would come under "Request" and what would come under "Order." Perhaps the person who wrote this made a mistake and then wanted to put that right or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, otherwise, according to military establishment, when you table -- when do you table a request and when do you issue an order?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I issue a request when I am not a superior to that person, the person I'm issuing it to, and an order is when I am that person's superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the commander of the 1st Brigade of the HVO, was he superior to the active military police?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for the unit that was under his area of responsibility for conducting military assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is P1972. It's a report from the 3rd Company of the Military Police Battalion, and it relates to the implementation of the order by Nedjeljko Obradovic. And Mr. Coric's Defence dealt with that in great detail. Now, could you tell me who this report was addressed to?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion Command, probably means the military police, the Military Police Administration, the brigade command, probably referring to the 1st HVO Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why this military police company is sending a report to the Military Police Administration?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that. It would be logical to go down the vertical chain of command through the 3rd Battalion and to send out the report through the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at the next document, which is 5D1054. My colleague has just told me that there was a mistake in the binder, because in the binder that document has the number P1054, where it should be 5D1054, which is the document in the binder of the Coric Defence. But we can also see it -- look at it on our screens. Now, on page 35, you, Mr. Pavlovic, confirmed that you had signed this document and sent it out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Referring to this order?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to tell you what a witness said about this order in the courtroom here. It was a protected witness who testified under the pseudonym of C, and his testimony was recorded on page 2257 [as interpreted] of the transcript. 55257 -- 22527 is the number, 22527. This document that you signed, he commented in the following way. I'm going to read out in English what he said and what was recorded in the transcript, to avoid mistakes: [In English] "As this is an order to a military police platoon, the one located in Stolac, this order never arrived in the company command. According to the book of rules which we have discussed just a while ago, all orders relating to combat activities, none of this would have been issued by a commander of a unit on the ground." [Interpretation] And then the question that followed was as follows: "So this order was issued contrary to the establishment of the military police?" And the answer: [In English] "Yes, both contrary to the establishment and without the knowledge of the company command within the composition of which the Stolac Platoon was." [Interpretation] Now, may we have your comments, Mr. Pavlovic, to this? Is it -- or, rather, was your order really unlawful, as has been suggested?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The military police platoon, which was in Stolac, I was able to engage for military police assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, do you know that the chief of the Military Police Administration -- whether he ever intervened --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I do apologise. I notice that the -- despite my respectful admonition or objection, my learned friend has slipped again, perhaps inadvertently, into some leading questions. I didn't object to the previous one, but any question that starts, "Do you know," I would just remind her to be careful in relation to leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, can you tell us whether the chief of the military police, Mr. Coric, ever intervened because of some unlawful act with respect to the military police in the area for which the 1st HVO Brigade was in charge up at the defence lines?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to avoid any misunderstanding, from the witness's answer it's not clear whether he didn't know about those things and thinks that Mr. Coric should have intervened or that, quite simply, he knew nothing about things like that, nor was he interested in whether Mr. Coric should have intervened or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that Mr. Khan is going to intervene with a leading question of that nature. I hope he'll rise to his feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Pavlovic, perhaps you can answer that before he does.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he intervened, and I didn't know about those higher echelons at all, what happened at the higher level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, had there been any complaints about the military police's conduct in the Stolac area, could you not have known about that? Was that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise? Could you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that Mr. Valentin Coric protested over the fact that you issued orders to the military police unlawfully in the Stolac area, without you knowing about it? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we don't know whether Mr. Valentin Coric knew which orders Mr. Pavlovic issued, because Mr. Pavlovic didn't send reports about the orders he issued. So the basis for this question, that Mr. Coric should intervene, he must have known what was going on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down and speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we would make some headway if the gentleman were to first explain to us how is that you have military police under him, directly under him, versus the other military police, what were -- even the division of labour, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm quite aware of the fact that my colleagues want to take up as much of my time as possible, but I will readily ask for more time and continue my redirect as I'd planned to do and carry on tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There seems -- we need some clarity. That's the whole purpose of it. So what is it? Because as I understand it, he should not have military police under him, and if he does, somehow either Obradovic created his own military police for himself and others, plus the other military police, or they're just using them as they will, willy-nilly. But we need to know what was the division of labour, how did they come into existence, and so on. And if we go step by step -- if we go step by step, maybe then we can see whether, you know, they were using them illegally or not. But also if I may -- just one second, Mr. President. Some of the questions assume facts which are not in evidence. They assume that this gentleman knows what exactly was being told to Mr. Coric and whether Mr. Coric, based on that information, was reacting. That's -- that's what's happening over here. So just step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, as to issues related to the military police, I'm sure that we're going to revisit the topic thoroughly when Mr. Coric calls his own witnesses. But now that you have ventured into this topic, be careful. Ask the witness what he knows and what his jurisdiction was over the military police so that everybody just doesn't intervene whilst it is a topic that the Judges are aware of as to the respective roles of the military police. We've seen hundreds of documents on the topic. So ask him what he knows, exactly, and then go along as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's how I asked my question, Your Honour, does he know that there were any complaints with respect to the conduct of the commanders in the military police. That was all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pavlovic, you can repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Complaints and criticism to the conduct of the military police, as far as I know, no, there weren't any. They went about their military police duties, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And on yesterday's transcript, on pages 25 and 26, and then 28 onwards, and in response to Judge Antonetti's questions, you said,

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVLOVIC
utterances.text: "If the active military police was attached to an HVO unit for the performance of police duties, then I was able to issue it orders to perform police assignments, but I could engage the military police in combat only on the basis of permission from my superior officer."

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You remember your answer, do you? Very well. Now, I am going to put to you what Witness C said on that same topic. Transcript page 22326: [In English] "If the commands, the orders, referred to the work of the military police, then we could carry them out. But if they were orders, whether they be written or oral, about tasks to be carried out up at the front-line, then we would not carry out those orders, and we would then ask the opinion of the Military Police Administration." [Interpretation] Can you tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, whether that is a correct description, or would you correct something in that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the description is a valid and correct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may at this stage perhaps just suggest that this may be a misleading question for the witness, because this relates to Dretelj and not Heliodrom, perhaps where his experience may lay regarding obtaining people for labour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this hasn't got anything to do with that. It's a matter of principle, pursuant to the command and the deployment of the military police, so nothing to do with any centre in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you tell us, Witness?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he's right, although in practice I never had the need to engage the military police, except to perform military police duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at another document which relates to you in the 3rd Brigade. It is P3770. That's right, P3770, which is an order from Valentin Coric, chief of the Military Police Administration, who is addressing you as commander of the 3rd Military Police Battalion, and he is re-subordinating a unit in order to secure the line around Heliodrom. He's re-subordinating two platoons made up of 32 military policemen. Now, Mr. Pavlovic, did you receive at that order to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this we can see that, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This name, Ivan Ancic, does it mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was commander -- I'm not sure whether it was a company at the time, but, anyway, a commander from the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would now like us to clarify an answer that you provided to Judge Trechsel's question. It's about document P3135. This is a document drafted on the 3rd of July, 1993, by the commander of the 1st Brigade of the HVO, and he is referring to his unlimited authority over civilian and military structures, in accordance with the extension of the zone of responsibility. If I may be allowed to draw my own conclusions, then Judge Trechsel wasn't too happy with your answer, so let me ask you on which day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I owe it to my status to protest. I am not "content" or "not content" with an answer. I'm not contrary to the parties. I do not want to solicit a specific answer when I ask a question, but I just want to know. So thank you. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right, but it seemed to me that it required some additional explanation because there was the -- the answer was provided with a certain smile.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So let me ask you, when did your responsibility in the 1st HVO Brigade end?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that is the day on which this order was issued; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will now return to the Prosecutor's cross-examination. Mr. Pavlovic, you tried to explain, on transcript pages 18 through 24, about the possible disarming of the Bregava Brigade, and that you never thought of disarming a brigade, because that would mean weakening the defence line. And a little later, you said that the Bregava Brigade did not hold the defence line at the features assigned to it very well. And Judge Trechsel asked you whether you could give an example, and you said that it was about Feature 690, which was lost in February 1993. Do you remember that reply, Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It should be toward the end of this binder. Take a look at document 4D1521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this will be very brief. I was amazed when you mentioned 690, Feature 690. I was amazed. What a fabulous memory, I thought. How is it that you remember that feature? Did you just keep it in mind, or do you remember, by the meter, how a feature is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must inform you now that Feature 690 is a place that I visit very often, and it is 300 metres away from my own farm. I own a piece of forest there, and I go hunting there, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you cook, also?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It may be funny, but it's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the first document, 4D1521. It is Miljenko Lasic's order. Let us look at item 2. Tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, which feature was the Bregava Brigade supposed to hold?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: TT -- that is trigonometric point 690.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us now look at document 4D477. 477, correct. This is a report by Mr. Slavko Puljic, based on the command issued by the commander of the Main Staff. He visited the positions of the 1st HVO Brigade and the Bregava Brigade in some zones, including Feature 690. Tell us, Mr. Pavlovic, how did it happen that an HVO officer also went to inspect the positions of the Bregava Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I mentioned this before. The control in the zone of responsibility of the Zone of Operations South-East Herzegovina can be conducted by an officer sent to do so by his commander or a superior officer, and since the Bregava Brigade was there, he had the right to inspect that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In item 1, Feature 690 is described as deserted for good. Was it really that way, Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the third -- last-but-three item. It says that: "Redistribution of the responsibility areas of the brigades must be conducted, since Bregava Brigade turned out to be unreliable." Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is fair and correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, today, toward the end of the first session, when my learned friend Mr. Kruger examined you, you said that the Bregava Brigade was relatively weak and unreliable, and we see corroboration of that here where Feature 690 is mentioned. Then the Prosecutor put it to you that it would be ridiculous to assume that such a weak brigade of the ABiH could take -- could assume an entire zone of responsibility of an HVO brigade. Do you remember that? I'll ask you a question about it. According to the plans that we saw, should the Bregava Brigade have assumed Capljina, Stolac, and other towns in this municipality or should it have done so in co-operation with someone else?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plans that they made, and that are available to us, and of which we knew at the time, were made in that operational unit, but probably the brigade should have been reinforced by substantial units in order to carry out these tasks. And it is -- it can clearly be seen there that it planned to perform these actions after being reinforced with Muslims in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If really all Muslims from the 1st HVO Brigade had joined the Bregava Brigade, would it have made it a respectable military force, in terms of numbers, at least?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, because the 1st Brigade at a certain time had as many as four and a half thousand men, and as far as I know, it was manned by Muslims, who made up about 50 per cent of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now I'll ask you a question about the osteopathic hospital. The document shown to you by Mr. Kruger -- I will now refer to documents which are already in evidence. P2612, 2612. Mr. Pavlovic, did we speak about the document during the proofing?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which contains that item 13, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Item 13 is a document by Nedjeljko Obradovic, and this document is a report of the EC monitors which mentions the evacuation of the hospital and states Bozo Pavlovic as the possible perpetrator of that evacuation. Well, never mind. We have no time.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour. Sorry, if I may interrupt, the exhibit being displayed at the moment is the one which is under seal, so if the other page can be displayed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't going to show the document, because I only have one question about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you haven't told us the whole story about the osteopathic hospital, and that's why I'm going to ask you now. In that document, you were tasked by Nedjeljko Obradovic, under item 13, to prevent the entry of new patients and to control the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you ever receive an order from Nedjeljko Obradovic to evacuate the patients from the osteopathic hospital?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, and I never did so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So if the statement in the document of the European Monitors, that you are the probable perpetrator of the evacuation of the patients from the osteopathic hospital, is it true or false?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PAVLOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is more probable for the sun to start shining now. It is most certainly false.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thus finish with my examination. Thank you, Mr. Pavlovic, for coming here and for replying to questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of my fellow Judges, I thank you for appearing on behalf of the Petkovic Defence to contribute to justice being done. Have a safe trip back home, and the usher is going to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honours, take one more minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you just want to say that you're very happy, fine, but you don't need to speak as to the merits of the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I just wanted -- because I was unable to greet anybody at the beginning, I just wanted to give my regards to everybody in the courtroom and thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You can leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next week, we are supposed to have a witness. There's no need to go into private session. The Trial Chamber is going to issue an oral ruling on motions for protective measures. All this is going to be filed shortly, as early as tomorrow. Therefore, you will have the entire and exhaustive decision. Mr. Stringer, did you want to speak? You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. It's too late and I definitely don't want to venture into this territory now, but it may be that at some point next week, or in one of the next witnesses, the Prosecution would like to make submissions to the Trial Chamber on the issues of new documents used in cross-examination, and also now on the issue of the scope of the cross-examination. It's our view that there are interventions which we think are not justified, and would, at the very least, like to seek the clarification of the Trial Chamber on how it's handling new documents presented on cross versus tendered into evidence, et cetera. It's a complicated issue, but it's one that we could benefit for some guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you will very well imagine, the Trial Chamber is aware of all these problems, and in our guide-lines we expressed ourselves very clearly. The Appeals Chamber confirmed our point of view. Now you revisit the issue. Since we often have Judges' meetings, we are going to address the issue once again, but I cannot preempt on the Trial Chamber's decision, but as far as I can see, everything is crystal clear. Two issues have to be settled, credibility or new topics. And I thought we had addressed all these issues already, but we heard you, my colleagues have heard you, and we are going to take all this on board. Are you happy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, we certainly accept and don't propose any revision or changes in the Trial Chamber's rulings, as well as the Appeal Chamber's. It's our view that the procedure that seems to be creeping in, which is that there are interventions every time a new document is presented to a witness on cross, it's our view that that is inconsistent with the guide-lines and the decisions that we have, and that this distinction between using a document on cross-examination versus subsequently tendering the document into evidence is being blurred, it's giving rise to interventions which, in our view, are not justified or in accordance with the current decisions that we recognise apply. So that's something that we think is becoming more and more of an issue. It's more and more troublesome to us, in terms of the Prosecution's constantly being asked -- or it's being asserted that the Prosecution has to justify using this or that document simply by presenting it to a witness in cross-examination. We don't think we have to do that. We think that certainly additional justifications and explanations are required if we tender the document, but that's what the issue is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, Mr. Stringer. If the document has not been included in the 65 ter list, you have to show good cause why you want to use the document. And if you present it, you basically -- it boils down to adding it to the 65 ter list. And the Appeals Chamber was very clear. You have to justify, to show reasons that there was no lack of diligence on your part, because it would be incredible that you would have had a document for four or five years and you get it out at the last minute. So, I mean, every Appeals Chamber decision is logical, is reasoned. I can speak about it for hours. It seems very clear to me, but not obviously for the Prosecution, who has problems with it. Yes, Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm most grateful. I am mindful of the time, and I'll be brief. I do note my learned friend had said that he wasn't wishing to litigate today the issue, notwithstanding the fact he did, of course, go into quite some detail. Your Honour has already pointed out that the Appeals Chamber decision is standing. This is a contentious issue, and it's one that is liable to take up quite some court time, if the Prosecution seek to reopen matters that we thought had been settled by the Appeals Chamber. Your Honours, there's no objection if my learned friends for the Prosecution wish to seek further clarification, but perhaps that can be done by way of written motion, to which the parties can respond. But, Your Honours, it is a matter that, if it's litigated in court, is going to be quite contentious and, I think, take quite a lot time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I was going to make a rather different suggestion from Mr. Khan. It's quite -- by -- Mr. Stringer, to be fair, made it clear at the outset he didn't particularly want to be drawn into submissions this afternoon, but, Your Honour, our position is that we're not accepting what he says this afternoon, but it is apparent that there is some need for clarification. But where I disagree with my learned friend Mr. Khan is that really it's not going to be resolved by written motions. That's likely to make it worse. We've all got our favourite procedures here, but this is an example of something which won't be worked out satisfactorily by written motions. What I was going to suggest, much more satisfactory, is that Mr. Stringer - and he usually has no objection to this sort of suggestion - if Mr. Stringer could just give some sort of note of -- just a checklist, some sort of skeleton of the particular points that he has in mind. We really ought to debate it in court. Your Honour, as a matter of fact, whether or not that would put Mr. Stringer under time pressure, probably not, because he's clearly thought about the matter. We do have tomorrow, actually. We really do have a whole day tomorrow where we could thrash this stuff out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, but the Judges' time is of the essence, is very precious, because we have to study thousands of pages, hundreds of thousands of pages, umpteen documents. Look at the number of documents through this witness alone. Mr. Stringer raises an issue that has already been settled by the Trial Chamber. We're going to discuss the issue among ourselves, and we will tell you whether we want to have oral litigation or use the written procedures. I usually have my answer, but there is four of us, so each of us has to express their opinions. There's no point in sort of discussing in a vacuum. If there is a legal problem, we can have a motion, a written decision, and possibly the Appeals Chamber. So let's not waste time on one new document that came up within one week. So that's the problem. So the Judges are going to discuss the issue, and we will tell you on Monday what we're going to do. Either we litigate it in court or we'll ask all the parties to file submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say something which I say with the greatest of respect, and it may not come as music to Your Honours' ears. But there is a point -- Your Honours refer to the valuable time of the Judges, but, Your Honours, there is a point at which, when counsel, and I mean Mr. Stringer here, but also clarification is needed on our side, there is a point at which when there is an issue which we, doing our jobs, really wish to have discussed and have Your Honours ruling on, that Your Honours' valuable time, really, with respect, might be made available to us to do that. And, Your Honour, that is what we are asking. What is extremely valuable is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, it is now 5 past 7.00. The interpreters have been working since the beginning of the hearing. We shall, therefore, continue, possibly, but the Judges will issue a decision, because you raise an issue that challenges a decision by the Appeals Chamber. That's all. That's the problem you now raise. The Trial Chamber is going to see whether there is any cause for review, and then we'll tell you what our decision is. We're not going to start the discussion now just because one of you raised an issue regarding one single document. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be continued on Monday, the 23rd day of November, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
